b: My employer, a large university, just announced a change in their recruitment policy. We must check a candidate’s references — two past supervisors plus their current supervisor — prior to a conditional offer of employment. Leadership is advising that all finalists (which could two, three, four, or even more candidates per job) should have their references checked prior to the final interview stage. This means that if we have multiple finalists, there would be at least one candidate whose current supervisor was asked for a reference, and then the candidate was not offered the job. Any candidate who refuses to provide a reference, including from their current supervisor, may not be considered for employment.

This makes me feel so slimy! I feel like it’s pretty standard for people to job search without alerting their current supervisor, and I have to imagine that at least some of them have managers/companies that would retaliate in some way when they find out their employee is job searching. I can’t wrap my head around why the university isn’t being more mindful of the impact this has on the candidate’s experience. I think we’ll miss out on a lot of great applicants who will self-withdraw because they don’t want to take the risk of having their current supervisor alerted to their job search without the security of an offer. Or, they’ll feel manipulated into complying/taking the risk. What’s your take?
Yes, this is a terrible and harmful policy.

It’s fine to want to check references on multiple candidates before making a final decision. References too often used as a just a rubber-stamp for a decision that’s already been made, whereas — when done well — they can be used to help make that decision. And if they’re genuinely being used to decide who to hire, not just as a perfunctory step for a decision that’s already been made (and that’s a big “if”), then it makes sense to talk to references for all your finalists, even though that means you’ll be talking to references for some people who you don’t end up extending an offer to.

But requiring references from current managers is always a bad idea. For many candidates, alerting their manager that they’re actively working to leave will jeopardize their current job. Some managers are punitive and will push people out earlier than they wanted to leave. Some won’t do that but it will affect things in more subtle ways (“I shouldn’t give Jane this important project because she’s probably leaving soon anyway” or “my raise budget doesn’t need to go to Jane since she’s about to leave, so I can use more of it on other team members”). And responding to that concern with, “Well, they are about to leave” doesn’t work — especially in this case where you know that some of those candidates won’t be getting an offer from you, but even in cases where they will (because there’s no guarantee that you’ll be able to come to terms on that offer and that they’ll accept it).
For those reasons, it’s very, very normal for job candidates not to offer their current manager as a reference, and for employers not to require it.
What your university is doing will endanger people’s sources of income, and you and your colleagues should push back on it.
